title: Output of the `knowledge.status` MCP tool
description:
The whole response, and the record of what this tool promises about a project's withheld half.

Six keys, always all six, and the split that matters is the one the measurement below makes. Four are identical between two projects differing only in an item the caller may not read — `projectId`, `itemCount`, `itemsByStatus`, `schemaVersion` — and two are not: `stateHash` and `appliedMigrations`, which identify the canonical state the counts were read from.

**The counts carry nothing about withheld content, not even a total.** `itemsByStatus` is computed over the surfaceable statuses alone and `itemCount` is the sum of that breakdown rather than the size of the store, so a project whose items are all retired answers `{}` and `0` — the counts a project holding nothing would give (SEC-13, T-17). The counts, and not the whole response: the next paragraph says which two fields still move. This is the claim `knowledge.get` makes in prose when it refuses to distinguish a withheld id from an absent one; a count that included the retired items would answer the same question with a number, and without the caller having to guess an id at all.

**`stateHash` and `appliedMigrations` move with any change to canonical state, including one that creates only withheld items.** That is measured, not conceded in the abstract: two projects built identically except for one extra migration creating a `rejected` item return the same `itemCount`, `itemsByStatus`, `projectId` and `schemaVersion`, and a different `stateHash` and `appliedMigrations` (Milestone 5, review round 8). So T-17's equality — one query against two corpora — holds for this tool's counts and not for its whole response, the way it does for `knowledge.search` and `knowledge.get`.

Both fields stay, and this file is where that decision is recorded rather than in a comment ([#19](https://github.com/theurian/theurian/issues/19)). The justification is per field below, and it is the same shape in both cases: neither carries a bit about *what* was withheld, and this tool takes one argument, so nothing about a request reaches either of them and there is no probe to vary — no extraction oracle, which is the property that made `snapshotId` publishable and `withheldSuperseded` not. A schema cannot enforce that relation between two responses; a validator sees one document. Read the paragraph above as a claim the project owes a differential test, and the constraints below as what this file does hold: which keys exist, and that no retired status may appear among them.

projectId.description: Echoed from the request. Always a registered id: an unregistered one is an error naming the ids that are registered, never an empty status (ADR-0002, SEC-13). Required on every call — there is no process-global current project, because with many agents sharing one daemon an implicit default reports one agent's project to another.

stateHash.description:
Which canonical state the counts were read from (FR-R5) — the identical string `knowledge.search` publishes as `retrieval.snapshotId`, so a caller holding one can compare it against the other without a second call and tell whether a search answered from the state this report describes.

Read from the same resolution of `.theurian/state/active.json` that chose the database these counts came from, not from a second read of the pointer. The two disagree exactly when `migrate apply` lands mid-request, and a hash naming a state the counts did not come from is worse than no hash at all.

**It moves for any change to canonical state, including a migration that creates only withheld items**, because it content-addresses the whole working tree by design (ADR-0016, ADR-0007): every migration file, every body file it references, and the schema and engine versions. It carries no bit about *what* changed — not a status, not an id, not a body — and it is query-independent by construction, which is the identical argument `snapshotId` carries and the reason FR-R5 publishes it at all. Removing it would remove the freshness contract this tool exists to serve. Accepted with that reasoning and the measurement in the top-level description ([#19](https://github.com/theurian/theurian/issues/19)).

itemCount.description:
The sum of `itemsByStatus`'s values, and deliberately not the number of items in the store.

Reporting the true total beside a filtered breakdown would hand back the withheld count exactly, by subtraction. A single aggregate withheld total was considered and rejected for the same reason a per-status one was: a caller who retires an item and watches one number move immediately afterwards has confirmed it, which is the oracle T-17 exists to close, only coarser.

So `0` here means "nothing you may see", not "nothing exists", and this number does not distinguish them — on purpose.

itemsByStatus.description:
How many items hold each status a caller may see. A key appears only when at least one item holds that status — a status with no items is absent rather than present with a zero — so `{}` is a valid and expected response.

**The three keys are exactly the surfaceable statuses** (`SURFACEABLE_STATUSES` in `theurian.domain.enums`), and `deprecated`, `superseded` and `rejected` can never appear. `additionalProperties: false` is what makes that a contract rather than a comment: a fourth key fails validation whatever it is named, so a breakdown that reported retired items under `other`, or under a relabelled bucket, is rejected too — it would leak the same quantity.

This tool takes no `includeUnapproved` flag, so the set is fixed rather than widened per caller. `draft` and `proposed` are counted here while `knowledge.search` withholds them by default: a count of work in progress is what a status report is for, and neither status is what SEC-13 withholds — retired knowledge is, and a rejected revision is where the secret that caused the rejection still lives.

approved.description: Items a team has agreed on. The only status default retrieval returns.

draft.description: Work in progress. Reachable through `knowledge.search` only with `includeUnapproved`.

proposed.description: Put forward and not yet decided. Reachable on the same terms as `draft`.

appliedMigrations.description:
How many migration files this project has applied — one per row of the canonical store's migration history, in the order they were applied. It is how a caller confirms that `theurian migrate apply` landed, which is the question this tool was added to answer.

A count of *files*, never of items. It moves identically whether a migration created an approved item, a draft, a rejected one, or no item at all, so it cannot be made to name a status, an id, or a body. Nothing about the request reaches it: `knowledge.status` takes only `projectId`, so there is no probe to vary and therefore no extraction oracle — the same property that made `snapshotId` safe to publish and a per-query count of withheld matches unsafe.

**It does move when a migration creating only withheld items lands**, which `stateHash` already does for the same input. The one bit it adds over the hash is direction — a migration was added rather than an existing one edited — and that bit is a fact about the project's own migration directory, which is Git-tracked in the caller's repository. Accepted on those terms rather than removed, bucketed, or recomputed over surfaceable items only: the first two break the use the field exists for, and the third would publish a number no user can reproduce from their own migration files ([#19](https://github.com/theurian/theurian/issues/19)).

schemaVersion.description:
The canonical store's SQLite schema version. Not the wire `protocolVersion`, and not the retrieval index's schema version — three different numbers, and this is the one that says how the knowledge database itself is laid out.

The version this daemon supports, which is also the version the database it just read holds: opening a store whose recorded version differs raises rather than reinterpreting the rows, so a response carrying this value is a response read from a store that matched it.

An input to `stateHash` (ADR-0017), so bumping it invalidates cached state instead of silently reinterpreting it — which is why two projects with identical knowledge and different schema versions do not share a hash.
